text:
Nearly five months into the war with Iran, 18 United States service members have been killed, and nearly 500 have been wounded. This week, Washington Democratic U.S. Sen. Patty Murray co-chaired a contentious Senate Appropriations Committee hearing. The focus was a $67 billion emergency supplemental funding request from the Department of Defense. Pentagon officials said they needed the funds to support the war and other military operations. KUOW’s Kim Malcolm spoke to Senator Murray about the hearing and other matters.

This interview has been edited for clarity.

Kim Malcolm: At the start of your questioning, you told Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth the administration was making an emergency request that might “be better understood as an attempt to skirt the normal appropriations process.” You told him the request did not make sense. What about it doesn't make sense?

Sen. Murray: Well, a lot of it doesn't make sense. The fact that they are asking for billions, I mean $70 billion, to fight a war that they never came to us with a strategy? They had different ideas every other day about why we needed to be there. There is no justification, and the American people don't support it. He didn't ask our allies.

To now come and say they need that amount of money from the American taxpayers to continue this. In order to do that, they needed to come to the committee and give very real information about what they were spending the money on, what was the strategy, what was the ending, what was the goal, and none of that was done.

What I was saying is that I look at their actual language and what they sent to me. They were asking for items for the Pentagon that should've been asked for us in our regular appropriations process. Now, why is that important? Because they are asking us for an emergency supplemental. That means not paid for. That means added to the debt of this nation, a cost that will be on us for years to come. It has to be paid for. We have to figure out what the balance is. If we do this, what is it going to cost us? How are we going to pay for it? What do we lose out? Instead, they are coming to ask for this money only by adding it to the debt, and to me, that was outrageous.

There are more Republican senators who are openly voicing concerns about the war against Iran now, but today, the Senate voted to block a resolution that would have directed President Trump to withdraw U.S. forces from that conflict. How do you see this playing out in the coming weeks?

Well, I will tell you, I was disappointed in the vote today, because we have had Republicans supporting us in the past on a resolution on whether we should support this war, and that didn't happen today. What I see Republicans doing is they're afraid of the president, and we're coming up on an election, and that scares them.

I have come to the conclusion that the only way we are going to stop this war, bring our troops home, and make those investments that we need for our military in a strategic war for the global needs that we do have, is to get the majority back so that we can have those votes and do that.

Is that what it's going to take in order for the United States to exit this conflict?

Well, that is what we kept asking Pete Hegseth and the White House, and they do not answer that. They skirt around. They blame Biden, who did not start this war, every other thing except how we get out of this.

So that is a really good question, and all of us need to understand that every day that we continue this war without justification and we lose our investments and use our investments is a day that we are really less safe because we aren't ready to defend ourselves in other areas of the world that we need to be prepared for.

So, the only way to do that is through how we control that money. That comes through the appropriations process in our budget, which will probably come after the election at this point. This is a time to vote. That's what I would say.

I want to ask you about election interference. Multiple states, including Washington, are pushing back on the Trump administration's efforts to impose restrictions on how elections are managed. The midterms are coming up, and I'm wondering what steps you're focused on to prevent election interference.

I think we should all be very concerned about that. President Trump has not been quiet about what his intentions are here. He gave an address to the nation last week that was totally crazy, but he is very clearly pushing the Senate and the House to pass his bill on voter legislation. He has made it very clear that he intends to use whatever means he has to win elections. That's not what a democracy is about. I think we all have to be aware of that.

Washington state has a system where we make sure everybody has the chance to vote. It's very safe and secure. We have mail-in ballots. He wants to prevent that. He wants to have ballots that can't get counted after Election Day. Well, if you live in rural Washington, or you didn't get to the mailbox in time, or you are serving overseas in any kind of capacity, that means it prevents people from being able to vote.

But we also have to remember on Election Day that in certain parts of this country, we have to make sure that we've got people out and ready to vote. And I have to tell you, Kim, because he has made these threats, I see people in many states where he is focused on who are standing up and saying, "I am going to vote. He is not going to prevent me from doing this." That's called standing up and fighting for democracy.

Political tensions are still high, and I'm wondering what your approach is right now with your Republican colleagues.

You know, I think that's such an important question. It's an important question for me here in the Senate with tensions high. It's important in families across this country who see somebody who doesn't agree with them as the enemy. I think we all have to take a breath, me in the Senate, families, people who live in neighborhoods, everybody, and say, "Just because somebody disagrees with me doesn't mean they are enemies.” It means that they have a difference of opinion.

I try to bring that with me to the Senate every day, and when someone says something that I don't agree with, I can point out that I disagree with them, but don't call them the enemy.
